This theme underwent extraordinary development. Fâtima-Sophia, sovereign of “humanity in its feminine form,” became the supreme figure of a Shiite teaching about divine Wisdom (sophiology). Writers would speak of the fâtimîya—the “Sophia-nature”—of the holy Imams. See our Terre céleste et corps de résurrection, pp. 114–119. ↩

See Kalâmi-Pîr, edited by W. Ivanow, p. 64 of the Persian text (Maliku's-salâm; Malik Shulim; Malik Yazdaq); and Haft Bâb or “Seven Chapters”, by Abû Ishaq Qûhistânî, edited by W. Ivanow, pp. 39–40 of the Persian text. Melchizedek's place in Ismaili Shiite gnosis deserves an extensive study. Qotboddîn Ashkevârî, a student of Mîr Dâmâd, identifies the third of the Zoroastrian Saoshyants, or Saviours, with the Twelfth Imam. It is therefore striking that Melchizedek is explicitly given the name of the first of the three Saoshyants. In the Haft Bâb, p. 41, line 1, the editor's question mark should be removed. The Persian spelling is perfectly correct and should be read Oslâdar: Avestan Ukhshyat-eretha → Pahlavi Hôshêtar → Persian Oshîdar. Raymond Panikkar's article “Eine Betrachtung über Melchisedek,” Kairos: Zeitschrift für Religionswissenschaft und Theologie, I (1959), pp. 5–17, repays reading. Panikkar writes from the standpoint of Catholic theology but senses that Melchizedek's priesthood embodies a universality capable of grounding a general theology of religions. Unfortunately, he seems unaware that Ismaili teachings on prophecy and divine wisdom had developed this idea centuries earlier. Nor does he seem to know that, within fifth-century Christianity itself, Melchizedek was, for the Melchizedekian Gnostics, the supreme figure in which the Logos appeared as divine—the Logos “apart from the flesh” (asarkos). This idea of divine manifestation provides a clue to the connection between the Melchizedek of Melchizedekian gnosis and that of Ismaili gnosis. ↩

Ismailism recognizes six great “speaking” prophets (Nâtiq, plural Notaqâ), each proclaiming a new religious Law; David is not included in this series. They represent the six days in which the religious cosmos, or sacred cosmos, was created. The seventh Nâtiq is the last Imam, who proclaims not a new sharî'at (religious Law), but the hidden meaning of the revelations. See our Trilogie Ismaélienne, index under “hexaéméron.” On the spiritual meaning of Creation's “six days,” see also our Herméneutique spirituelle comparée (above, p. 27, n. 4). ↩

See 'Azîz Nasafî, Tahqîq-e nobowwat o walâyat, quoted in Tarâ'iq, vol. I, p. 259. Sa'doddîn Hamûyeh (or Hamû'î) was 'Azîz Nasafî's teacher. His still-unpublished work gives spiritual testimony of fundamental importance to the Twelfth Imam's “invisible presence.” See also 'Azîz Nasafî, Le Livre de l'Homme parfait, Persian text published by the late Marijan Molé (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. XI), Tehran–Paris, 1962. ↩

The oldest document on this subject appears to be Mas'ûdî's Kitâb Ithbât al-wasîya (d. between 333 and 346 AH, or 944 and 957 CE). See Colloque sur le shî'isme imâmite, 1968 (Publications du Centre d'histoire des religions de l'Université de Strasbourg), C. Pellat's paper, pp. 69 ff., and our comments, p. 90. The same names appear, arranged in ingenious diagrams, in Haydar Âmolî. On Ismailism, see our Herméneutique spirituelle comparée, p. 173, n. 169; p. 175, n. 190; etc. ↩

Over the centuries, Shiites had filled the Baqî' cemetery with splendid monuments of devotion—domes and shrines. After the Wahhabis took power in Arabia, following their entry into Mecca in 1924, they demolished the entire complex on puritanical grounds, leaving it in ruins. During his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1956, the Iranian sovereign, accompanied by his whole entourage, paid a long visit to Baqî', stopping at the sites of tombs revered by Shiites. Promises were made to restore what could be restored. The visit attracted particular attention because an Iranian sovereign had not been seen there for a very long time; Iranian periodicals published many illustrations of the occasion. ↩

The Dawâzdeh Imâm (“Doxology of the Twelve Imams”), attributed to Nasîroddîn Tûsî, appears, among other places, in the great collection of prayers compiled by the famous theologian Moh. Bâqer Majlisî, Kitâb Zâd al-ma'âd (Provisions for the Return), lithographic edition, Tehran, 1352/1933, large octavo, 588 pages (Arabic and Persian). Our text appears in the margins of pp. 207–227. It must not be confused with a much longer text, the Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a (spiritual visitation of the Twelve Imams), which goes back to the Tenth Imam, 'Alî Naqî. The Ziyârat brings together the attributes ascribed to the Imams in earlier hadîth. In Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's profound, densely argued commentary (Tabriz edition, 1276/1860; see below, vol. IV, Book V), it becomes a complete exposition of the divine wisdom and spirituality associated with the Imams. On this work, see our report in the Annuaire 1968–1969 of the Religious Sciences Section, pp. 151–154. The attributes by which the Imams appear to Shiite religious consciousness are, in themselves, the foundation for spiritual interpretation of the Qur'an. ↩

See our Trilogie Ismaélienne, index under “shî'isme,” and Histoire de la philosophie islamique, vol. I, Chapter II in its entirety. Readers will understand why, to complete that latter work, we must first perform the thankless labour of editing texts, most of which still survive only as manuscripts. The article mentioned in this book's preface outlines the programme we have tried to pursue over the years in our teaching at the École des Hautes Études. Meanwhile our colleague Sayyed Jalâloddîn Ashtiyânî, professor at the University of Mashhad, is preparing an Anthologie des philosophes iraniens from the seventeenth century to the present, which is to include some fifty Shiite thinkers. ↩

This letter of Imam Ja'far is quoted at length in Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr (above, p. 27, n. 4), pp. 12–14. The people criticized by the Imam are followers of Abû'l-Khattâb and, in the commentator's secondary application, the reformed Ismailis of Alamût. Certain hadîth make the strange assertion that “Prayer is a person,” “Fasting is a person,” and so on. Some followers have used these statements to claim that knowing this person releases them from actually observing religious practices. What lies behind the question, however, is a metaphysics of being that determines the relation between the name of an action (nomen actionis) and the name of its agent (nomen agentis). It concerns personal archetypes, not abstract essences. See our studies “Rituel sabéen et exégèse Ismaélienne du rituel” (Eranos-Jahrbuch XIX, pp. 229 ff.) and “Le Temps cyclique dans le mazdéisme et dans l'ismaélisme” (Eranos-Jahrbuch XX, pp. 208 ff.), which examine important passages from Nasîr Tûsî's Tasawworât. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, in his major commentary on the Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a (p. 378), resolves the issue admirably through the idea of walâyat: the faithful are created through a ray of the light that constitutes the being of their Imams. ↩
For a brief account of the circumstances, see our Histoire de la philosophie islamique, pp. 114 and 138. ↩

See our article “Huitième centenaire d'Alamût,” Mercure de France, February 1965, pp. 285–304. It sketches the geographical setting of the preceding events and translates the “Great Proclamation” of Imam Hasan, 'alâ dhikrihi's-salâm. ↩

This text appears in Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's great commentary on Ibn Bâbûyeh's (d. 381/991) Kitâb al-Tawhîd, Chapter II, thirty-fifth hadîth, third matlab, fol. 136b (Persian manuscript). A follower had come to speak with the Tenth Imam, 'Alî Naqî, whom the Abbasid authorities were holding prisoner in the military camp of Samarra. The long record of their conversation amounts to a complete statement of Imami Shiite faith. Qâzî Sa'îd repeatedly returns to the Imamate as a purely spiritual kingship. This matters because impoverished philosophies of history too often try to “explain” a turn toward the spiritual realm and hopes of the end times as compensation for political frustration. Quite apart from entirely missing the point, such explanations overlook the fact that Qâzî Sa'îd was writing at the height of the Safavid period, when Shiism could hardly be said to suffer political frustration. Just as the Imams in the hadîth always discuss religious matters with their disciples, our thinkers have always known that the Imamate's meaning transcends all worldly politics: its essential dimension concerns the ultimate destiny of humanity. ↩

The threefold shahâdat, or declaration of faith, that makes an ordinary moslim (Muslim) into a mu'min (a faithful Shiite believer) therefore comprises affirmation of divine oneness (tawhîd), affirmation of the prophetic mission (nobowwat), and affirmation of the Imams' walâyat. See, among others, Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr, Moqaddamât I, Maqâlat II, pp. 23 ff. ↩

There is a necessary connection between Shiite negative, or apophatic, theology (tanzîh) and its teaching about the Imams. This teaching assigns the Imams an “epiphanic function” (mazharîya): they make manifest not the divine Essence (dhât) itself, but God's action or “energy” (fe'l). See our paper “Imâmologie et philosophie” (Strasbourg conference, 1968; above, p. 65, n. 46). Negative theology is set out with complete rigour in a long sermon (khotba) delivered at Merv by the Eighth Imam, 'Alî Rezâ, and included in Ibn Bâbûyeh's Kitâb al-Tawhîd, Chapter II, second hadîth. Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's commentary on this text is fundamental. ↩

In his Jâmi' al-asrâr (published in La Philosophie shî'ite, cited above, p. 56, n. 29), pp. 424–425, Haydar Âmolî recalls a moving exchange between the Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sâdiq, and Abû Hanîfa, who had once been his pupil. Abû Hanîfa asks the Imam to come to Kufa and forbid people to insult the memory of the Prophet's Companions. “The Imam: They would not accept what I told them. — Abû Hanîfa: How could they refuse to accept it from you, when you are a descendant of God's Messenger? — The Imam: You yourself are the first to disregard me. You entered my house without my permission. You sat down without my asking you to. You speak without consulting me. I hear you argue by syllogisms? — Abû Hanîfa: Yes. — The Imam: Beware, O No'mân! The first to make a syllogism was Iblîs [Satan], when he was ordered to bow before Adam. ‘You created me from fire,’ he said, ‘whereas you created him [Adam] from clay.’” (The Imam then asks Abû Hanîfa a series of questions about religious law, fiqh, and Qur'anic commentary, tafsîr. Every time Abû Hanîfa answers, the Imam asks, “Why, then … ?” until Abû Hanîfa's position becomes impossible to defend.) Haydar Âmolî continues with magnificent vehemence: “This is how that man [Abû Hanîfa] spoke to the Pole of poles during his lifetime. Yet this is the very man whom the gnostic ['ârif, Dâwûd Qaysarî] counts among the most eminent Friends of God [Awliyâ]! I call God to witness: it is an enormous imposture. Truly, the hostility toward Shiites and toward certain other Sufis arises from absurdities of this kind. If I were not afraid of making this too long, I would explain some of their principles [osûl] and their derivative rulings [forû'], which would allow us to judge their position. But it is better to be silent.” ↩

Even if the First Imam did not actually deliver this sermon at Kufa, an eternal Imam did, at some point, speak it within Shiite consciousness; from the standpoint of religious experience, that is what matters. In fact the sermon brings together numerous statements scattered through hadîth regarded as especially authentic. A thinker as exacting as Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, who himself wrote a commentary on it, accepted the sermon as authentic. It also appears identical to the Khotbat al-iftikhâr (Dharî'at, vol. III, no. 984), already mentioned by Ibn Shahr-Ashûb; a commentary by Hasan Sabbâh, founder of Alamût (d. 518/1124), is also reported (see Kalâmi-Pîr, edited by W. Ivanow, pp. 79–81 of the Persian text). The Khotbat al-Bayân belongs to a group of sermons that give especially powerful expression to Shiite gnosis. See Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, Kitâb Asrâr al-Hajj (above, p. 98, n. 66), Chapter V. It begins with a long hadîth of the Sixth Imam on the secret of the Black Stone (see our “La Configuration du Temple de la Ka'ba comme secret de la vie spirituelle,” Eranos-Jahrbuch XXXIV, pp. 129 ff.). Qâzî Sa'îd writes: “What comes to mind in trying to explain this mysterious account is that the best explanation is that the covenant [mîthâq] was received in several successive dwellings or levels, as the thing descended from the higher heavens to the lower heavens” (fol. 183). Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr draws the same teaching from a long hadîth of the Sixth Imam, which says, among other things: “Then He created the angels, revealed Himself to them, and received from them the covenant [mîthâq]: toward Himself with respect to divine lordship [robûbîyat], toward Mohammad with respect to prophecy [nobowwat], and toward 'Alî with respect to walâyat” (p. 29). There was therefore a covenant before the one required of Adam, ancestor of earthly humanity (Qur'an 7:171). We shall also have occasion to note that the angels ordered to bow before Adam (Qur'an 2:28) were only the lower angels (malâ'ika), not the four angels supporting the Throne ('arsh), nor those called al-'âlûna (“the Sublime Ones”). These latter are the Veils, the Lights of the Haqîqat mohamma-dîya (the eternal Muhammadan Reality) of which the Throne is composed; it was precisely before these Lights shining within Adam that the lower angels bowed. Nor did the command concern the Karûbîyûn (Cherubim), called the “angels of the Veils.” See Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, commentary on Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a (above, n. 48), p. 117. Like Ismaili teachings about Adam, Imami teachings recognize Adam on several levels: Adam al-akbar, the greater or cosmic Adam; Adam al-asghar, the lesser or little Adam; and so forth. ↩

We must mention here one of Mollâ Sadrâ's most powerful passages, commenting on Qur'an 7:171 in his great commentary on Kolaynî, Sharh al-Osûl min al-Kâfî, Tehran, n.d., p. 321. Sadrâ speaks of the different levels on which souls become manifest: the world of Intelligences, the Malakût (spiritual kingdom), the mundus imaginalis or barzakh (intermediate imaginal world), and finally the physical world. He invokes Plato's teaching on the pre-existence of souls and finds it entirely consonant with Qur'an 7:171. Yet he believes that “pre-existence” alone is not enough: one must recognize that “there” souls have another mode of being and another way of appearing. The zohûr referred to in the verse, the “loins” that contained Adam's descendants, were precisely the Intelligences, the 'Aqûl, regarded as their “fathers” in their pre-existence on the level of the world of Intellect. We shall return to this interpretation in a book devoted specifically to Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. For now, let us simply note that Mollâ Sadrâ was not the first to find an agreement between Platonism and Shiism concerning the pre-existence of souls. Seven centuries earlier, Ibn Bâbûyeh had already taught pre-existence, in language with striking Platonic echoes, in his Kitâb al-I'tiqâdât (Book of Beliefs), a fundamental work of Shiite thought. ↩

I, pp. 401–402. Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr, p. 26, quotes it from Sadûq Ibn Bâbûyeh's Ma'ânî al-akhbâr; see Safînat, II, p. 29. A simple example will help. Suppose the natural meaning, the literal wording of the Word, seems to yield no divinely inspired revelation. We may see this failure in the words of those who declare: “Out of Galilee no prophet arises” (John 7:53, as cited here). But perhaps this denial takes place within the very household of the Word, where the Word is profaned by its own people. That is what is suggested by the words: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13:13, as cited here). “Galilee” and “Jerusalem” thereby become symbols whose meanings radiate in inexhaustible waves. Even when a symbol has been explained, it always calls for fresh interpretation, because it remains less than the mystery to which it points. On the two Gospel passages, see W. Cairns Henderson's fine essay “The Prophet of Nazareth of Galilea,” New Church Life, Bryn Athyn, Pennsylvania, April 1965, pp. 145 ff. ↩
